title: Design patterns used in iOS
summary: A design pattern is a well-known solution to a common problem. iOS uses many: Singleton, Delegate, Observer, Coordinator, Factory, Builder, Adapter, Strategy and Facade.
body: **Singleton:** one shared instance (`URLSession.shared`, `UserDefaults.standard`). Easy, but it is global state that hides dependencies and makes tests hard. If you use one, hide it behind a protocol and inject it.
**Delegate:** one object acts on behalf of another (`UITableViewDelegate`).
**Observer:** many listeners get notified of changes (NotificationCenter, KVO, Combine, `@Observable`).
**Coordinator / Router:** an object that owns navigation, so screens do not know about each other. Makes flows reusable and deep links easy.
**Factory:** one place that creates objects, often with their dependencies (`makeProfileViewController(userID:)`).
**Builder:** build a complex object step by step (`URLComponents`, request builders).
**Adapter:** wrap a third-party API behind your own protocol so you can swap it (analytics, image loading SDKs).
**Strategy:** swap algorithms behind one interface (different pricing rules, different caching policies).
**Facade:** a simple front for a complicated subsystem (one `PaymentService` over several payment SDKs).
**Dependency Injection:** give an object what it needs instead of letting it create or find it (see the DI entry).
keyPoints: Know at least: Singleton, Delegate, Observer, Coordinator, Factory, Adapter, Strategy.
Singletons are fine for stateless global services but should be injectable.
Coordinator removes navigation from view controllers.
Adapter around third-party SDKs keeps them replaceable and testable.
Always explain the problem a pattern solves, not just its name.
